name: SVG
quick_answer: SVG — Scalable Vector Graphics format for resolution-independent vector artwork, icons, and illustrations that scale cleanly at any size.
definition: SVG is an image file format. Scalable Vector Graphics format for resolution-independent vector artwork, icons, and illustrations that scale cleanly at any size. It is commonly used in workflows that require reliable image handling and is supported by a wide range of applications and online tools.

use_cases.title: Logos and brand identity assets
use_cases.text: SVG is the preferred format for logos and brand assets because it scales perfectly from a small favicon to a billboard without any quality loss.

use_cases.title: Icons and interface graphics
use_cases.text: SVG is widely used for UI icons in web applications and design systems because the files are tiny and render sharply at every screen density.

use_cases.title: Data visualizations and charts
use_cases.text: SVG is used for interactive charts, graphs, and infographics on the web because it can be manipulated with CSS and JavaScript.

use_cases.title: Responsive web illustrations
use_cases.text: SVG illustrations adapt to any container size, making them ideal for responsive web pages and high-DPI displays.

use_cases.title: Animated and interactive graphics
use_cases.text: SVG supports CSS and SMIL animation as well as JavaScript-driven interactions, enabling rich visual experiences without video.

advantages.title: Infinite scalability
advantages.text: SVG images scale to any size without pixelation or quality loss because they are defined by mathematical paths, not pixels.

advantages.title: Very small file sizes for line art
advantages.text: SVG files for icons and logos are typically a few kilobytes, far smaller than equivalent raster images at the same visual quality.

advantages.title: Editable and accessible text
advantages.text: SVG markup is human-readable XML, making it easy to edit in a text editor, inspect in browser devtools, and index by search engines.

advantages.title: CSS and JavaScript integration
advantages.text: SVG elements can be styled with CSS and animated or manipulated with JavaScript directly in the browser DOM.

advantages.title: Resolution-independent on all displays
advantages.text: SVG renders sharply on standard, Retina, and high-DPI screens without requiring separate image assets for different pixel densities.

limitations.title: Not suitable for photographs
limitations.text: SVG is a vector format and is not designed for photographic images with complex color gradients or camera-captured detail.

limitations.title: Complex SVGs can be slow to render
limitations.text: SVG files with many paths, filters, or animations can cause rendering performance issues in browsers when used at scale.

limitations.title: Security risk with embedded scripts
limitations.text: SVG files can contain JavaScript and external references, making user-submitted SVGs a potential security risk if not sanitized.

limitations.title: Limited support in some email clients
limitations.text: Most email clients do not render inline SVG, requiring fallback raster images for HTML email campaigns.

comparisons.title: SVG vs PNG
comparisons.text: SVG is a resolution-independent vector format ideal for logos and icons at any size, while PNG is a raster format best suited to detailed photographs and screenshots.

comparisons.title: SVG vs PDF
comparisons.text: SVG is optimized for interactive and scalable web graphics and is rendered by browsers natively, while PDF is a document format designed for fixed-layout print and sharing.

comparisons.title: SVG vs WEBP
comparisons.text: SVG is a vector format that scales infinitely and is ideal for line art and icons, while WebP is a raster format optimized for photographic compression on the web.

faq.question: What is an SVG file?
faq.answer: An SVG (Scalable Vector Graphics) file is an XML-based vector image format that describes shapes, paths, and text mathematically rather than as pixels.

faq.question: Is SVG a vector or raster format?
faq.answer: SVG is a vector format. It stores image data as mathematical descriptions of shapes, so it scales to any size without loss of quality.

faq.question: Can SVG be used directly on websites?
faq.answer: Yes, SVG can be embedded directly in HTML or referenced as a src attribute, and all modern browsers render it natively.

faq.question: Can I edit SVG files in a text editor?
faq.answer: Yes, SVG is plain XML text. You can open and edit it with any text editor, though vector design tools like Inkscape or Figma are more practical.

faq.question: When should I use SVG instead of PNG?
faq.answer: Use SVG for logos, icons, and line art that need to scale at multiple sizes. Use PNG for photographs and complex raster images.

faq.question: Can SVG files contain animation?
faq.answer: Yes, SVG supports animation using CSS transitions, SMIL animation attributes, or JavaScript, making it useful for interactive web graphics.
